sections.h2: Which Madison County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Three offices share the job, and none of them does all of it. The Assessor of Property values the land and buildings, the County Commission and the Jackson City Council set rates, and the Trustee collects the county's bill. The assessor's own page says the office neither sets the rate nor collects tax.

  • Trustee: Billy Burkhead, 100 E. Main St., Suite 107, Jackson, TN 38301, phone (731) 423-6027, open weekdays, 9:00 to 5:00, on the courthouse's first floor.
  • Assessor of Property: Frances Hunley, Suite 304 on the courthouse's third floor, phone (731) 423-6063, open weekdays, 8:30 to 5:00.
  • City of Jackson Revenue Office: bills tax for houses inside the city. A city address owes both the county and the city.

The county's Payment of Taxes page says the Assessor's office neither accepts payments nor mails bills. It supplies owner names and mailing addresses to the offices that do, so a moved owner should update the address with the Assessor.

sections.h2: What does the Madison County landscape look like to a seller?
sections.html:
Madison County lies in West Tennessee, and Jackson is its seat and its biggest city. It was founded in 1821 and named for James Madison. It covers 559 square miles, nearly all land, and borders Gibson, Carroll, Henderson, Chester, Hardeman, Haywood and Crockett counties. Interstate 40 crosses it along with US 45, US 70 and US 412.

Several landmarks shape how people describe the area. Pinson Mounds, one of the largest Woodland period mound complexes in the country, lies in the county, and Lake Graham, a 500-acre reservoir, sits five miles east of Jackson. Beyond Jackson, the county includes Medon, Three Way, Beech Bluff, Pinson and parts of Humboldt and Mercer. The Jackson-Madison County School System serves public school families, Lane College and Union University are in the county, and West Tennessee Healthcare runs the public hospital system. Jackson Regional Airport took that name in 2025.

Census Bureau QuickFacts for Madison County:

  • Population on July 1, 2025: 100,790, versus 98,823 at the 2020 census
  • Housing units: 44,744, with 62.0% owner-occupied from 2020 to 2024
  • Typical owner-occupied house, by value: $211,800
  • Median gross rent: $1,123, and median household income $60,042
  • Building permits in 2025: 236

sections.h2: When does the next Madison County reappraisal happen?
sections.html:
The next reappraisal is set for 2027, and the last one was in 2022. The Assessor's page cites Tennessee Code 67-5-1601 as the reason the county has to reappraise on a schedule. Madison County works on a five-year cycle, and between cycles the office inspects about one-third of the parcels each year for changes to land or buildings.

The office posts a market indicator on that page. It reports a median residential sale price of $251,450 as of January 2026, against $212,500 at the 2022 reappraisal, which it describes as roughly an 18.33% rise. That gap is the main reason an owner should expect a higher appraised value in 2027. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value and commercial property at 40 percent, per the county's FAQ.

Assessment Change Notices go out by law, usually in May, and only to owners whose value moved up or down from the prior year. Notices that come back undeliverable are common, so owners who moved in the last two or three years should call the office to fix the address.

sections.h2: When are Madison County tax notices sent, and how do I pay?
sections.html:
Notices should reach owners in the first week of October, and the Assessor says taxes cannot be paid early. Search and pay online at paymadisontaxes.com, call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 or stop by the courthouse. The Trustee's site notes that the office collects only county property tax, and the County Commission sets the rate.

Tennessee taxes follow the owner of record on January 1 for the whole year. That means the county's public records will not show a mid-year purchase on the new owner's tax bill. The Assessor's FAQ also warns that tax figures on a closing statement are typically estimates, especially for a closing before October 1, and tells buyers and sellers to ask the closing attorney who pays what. For the delinquency date and interest schedule, ask the Trustee directly, since both are set by the county's collection office.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Madison County assessment?
sections.html:
First call the Assessor at (731) 423-6063 and ask to verify the property record. The office reviews the property card, takes down your reasons, and has a field appraiser recheck it. If that does not settle it, the next step is the Madison County Board of Equalization.

The board is five property owners from the county and the City of Jackson. By law it hears appeals on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, and the county begins scheduling appointments in the last two weeks of May. One FAQ elsewhere on the county site says the board sits for the first week to ten days of June, so confirm the dates with the Assessor. The board can only hear the current tax year: the county's example is that 2025 taxes cannot be appealed in 2026.

The county asks residential owners to bring comparable sales from the year or two before the tax year, a recent paid appraisal and photos of the exterior and interior. Owners of income property are asked for three years of leases, rent rolls, income and expenses, appraisals, sales contracts, closing statements and construction costs. Refusing to supply those documents can cost the right to introduce them before the State Board. The appeal page adds that the State Board filing carries a fee, with $10 to $17 of it nonrefundable, and that you must pay at least the undisputed part of the tax before it turns delinquent. The State Board's number is 615-401-7883.

sections.h2: What tax relief does the Madison County Trustee offer?
sections.html:
The Trustee takes applications for the state's relief program for elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners, disabled veterans and widows or widowers of disabled veterans. Call the Trustee's office at (731) 423-6027 for the current requirements.

Applicants should bring a driver's license, a Medicare card, a Social Security card and proof of income for the applicant, spouse and every owner of the property. A mobile home owner also needs a copy of the title or bill of sale. Because the dollar limits change from year to year, ask the Trustee for the current income cap and filing deadline before assuming you qualify.

sections.h2: What should a Madison County seller do about tax before closing?
sections.html:
Ask the Trustee, and the Jackson Revenue Office if the house is in the city, for a written balance before you list. The January 1 rule means the owner of record on that date is the name on the bill even after a fall closing. Whether the buyer reimburses the seller for the unexpired months is something the closing attorney settles on the statement.

Sellers with older balances, an estate to settle or a pending appeal can raise those items with the closing attorney before the contract date. Paying an old balance first keeps the file simple and prevents a delay at the table.

faqs.q: Do I pay both the county and the city on a Jackson house?
faqs.a: Yes. A house inside Jackson owes Madison County tax through the Trustee and City of Jackson tax through the city's Revenue Office. A house outside the city limits owes the county tax only.

faqs.q: When is the next reappraisal in Madison County?
faqs.a: The next reappraisal is 2027. The last one took effect in 2022, and the Assessor's office estimates the median home sale price has risen about 18.33% since then, so expect values to move.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Madison County taxes early?
faqs.a: No. The Assessor's FAQ says taxes cannot be paid early, and notices should arrive in the first week of October. Call the Trustee at (731) 423-6027 if yours is missing.

faqs.q: Whose name is on the tax bill after I sell?
faqs.a: The January 1 owner stays on the county's records for the entire year, so the bill may carry the seller's name after closing. The closing attorney divides the cost between buyer and seller, and the Assessor suggests asking that attorney how.

faqs.q: How many weeks does the Board of Equalization meet?
faqs.a: About two weeks in June. The county page says hearings run on weekdays during the first two weeks of June, with appointments taken in the last two weeks of May. Call (731) 423-6063 for this year's schedule.
